name: The Lime Tree of Leliceni

location.address: In front of the Roman Catholic church, Leliceni, Harghita county, Romania

access: Free, in the churchyard of the village's Roman Catholic church, open ground
transport: Village of Leliceni, a few km north of Miercurea Ciuc/Csíkszereda; no public transport detail found, best reached by car
story:
In 2011 a lime in front of a village church in the Szekler hills of Transylvania was voted European Tree of the Year, with 23,298 votes. It had won Romania's own contest first. Leliceni, Csíkszentlélek in Hungarian, sits a few kilometres north of Miercurea Ciuc, and the tree has stood before its Roman Catholic church for roughly five hundred years: the contest and Romanian national news both date its planting to the early 1500s. It is about 20 metres tall and 3.9 metres round, and the county declared it a natural monument in 1992.

Its real claim is civic rather than botanical. By local tradition the villagers ringed the trunk with log benches and sat under the crown to argue out the affairs of the village, and wooden benches are said to stand there still. A tree that has served as the parish meeting room for centuries has heard more local politics than most town halls.

Local tradition also says the tree and the church came through a Tatar raid that burned the village around them. Sources place that raid at various points in the 1600s and none documents it, so take it as the story the village tells rather than as history.

The most recent reports we have found date from the contest years, around 2011 and 2012. If you have stood under it since, tell us how it is doing.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its place directly in front of the village's Roman Catholic church and by a trunk 3.9 metres round. It is the big lime in the churchyard.

best_time.label: early July, when the lime flowers and the churchyard smells sweet

name: The Zagradski Plane (Zagradski Chinar)

location.address: Zagrade quarter of Garmen, opposite St. George's Church, on the road from Gotse Delchev to Marchevo, Blagoevgrad region, Bulgaria

access: Free, standing on open ground in the Zagrade quarter of the village, opposite the church
transport: Garmen village, on the Gotse Delchev to Marchevo road; no rail, nearest reasonable public transport is the intercity bus to Gotse Delchev, then local onward transport
story:
Two plane trees stand opposite the church of St. George in Garmen, and the famous one is the older of the pair. The Zagradski Plane took second place in European Tree of the Year 2011 with 18,374 votes, a year after winning Bulgaria's national contest, and it appears on the municipality's coat of arms.

It is 24 metres tall and 10.46 metres round. How old it is depends on who you ask: the contest and a Bulgarian tourist guide say more than 600 years, while Bulgarian Wikipedia gives about 650, from a 1968 survey estimate. Even the year it became protected is disputed, 1961 in one source and 1968 in two others. Somewhere between 550 and 700 years covers every reading.

The same 1968 survey put the tree beside it at around 300. Together they are the Zagrade planes, standing in what was once a separate village and is now a quarter of Garmen, on the road from Gotse Delchev to Marchevo.

The legend is better than the paperwork. Ottoman janissaries are said to have set the tree alight to punish a villager who warned others that the water had been poisoned, and the villagers put the fire out, leaving a scar. Nobody has documented it. What is documented is the use: weddings and village gatherings under the crown, storks roosting in season, and in 2017 a Rotary Club project that turned the ground around the two trees into an open-air museum.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 10.46 metres round and far thicker than the younger plane beside it. It stands on the Gotse Delchev to Marchevo road, directly opposite St. George's Church in the Zagrade quarter.

name: The Plane Tree of Letenye

location.address: Castle park (Andrássy-kastély park), Szabadság tér 15, Letenye, Zala county, Hungary

access: Free, standing in the public castle park in the centre of Letenye
transport: Letenye town centre, Zala county, near the Croatian border; nearest train station Letenye, short walk to the castle park
story:
For centuries the people of Letenye have used one plane tree as the place to meet, to court, to quarrel and to settle business. In 2010 a local civic association campaigned it to victory as Hungary's Tree of the Year, and a year later it came third in Europe with 8,836 votes.

It stands in the castle park at Szabadság tér 15, the 5.6-hectare grounds of a Baroque castle the Szapáry family built in the mid-18th century and the Andrássy family later held. The tree is 20 metres tall and 6.15 metres round, and its crown spreads more than 36 metres, nearly twice as wide as the tree is high.

Its age is where the sources part. The contest and Hungary's national contest site both say about 500 years; a 2015 local news article says about 300. Neither figure rests on a ring count or a planting record, so the honest answer is somewhere between the two.

The town once held dances in its shade. They were stopped to protect the roots, which is a rare case of a town giving up a party for a tree. Couples still come for wedding photographs, and the plane has turned up in poems, letters and paintings.

In November 2014 vandals damaged a plaque at the tree, and the town took it personally enough to make the local news. That report is also the latest we have found describing it alive and standing. If you have seen it since, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the crown, more than 36 metres across, and a trunk 6.15 metres round. It stands in the castle park on Szabadság tér, and it is the park's one famous plane.

name: The Old Lime Tree of Felsőmocsolád

location.address: In the estate forest about 1km east of Bánó Mária Castle, beside the Malom-árok stream, Felsőmocsolád, Somogy county, Hungary

access: Free, standing in the estate forest near the Bánó Kastélyszálló (Bánó Castle Hotel); treated as a public tourist attraction by two independent hiking/tourism sites, with no restriction mentioned, though it sits on grounds historically tied to the castle estate
transport: Felsőmocsolád village, Somogy county; no rail; nearest reasonable public transport is a regional bus to Somogy villages, then on foot/by car to the forest site about 1km from the castle
story:
Local families bring their newborns to this lime, and older children climb through its hollow trunk to prove they are brave. It won European Tree of the Year in 2012 with 11,158 votes, a year after winning Hungary's national contest.

It stands in the forest of the former Kacskovics-Bánó estate, about a kilometre east of Bánó Mária Castle, beside the Malom-árok stream. It is 20 to 25 metres tall and put at roughly 400 years old. A Hungarian hiking directory records its circumference as 11.9 metres, a figure that says less about one trunk than about the shape of the whole thing: three thick limbs rising from a hollow base. Read the number as a measure of that base rather than of an ordinary trunk.

The village has a legend to match. A great storm, lightning and an explosion of gas are said to have burned the surrounding forest into a chasm called Hell's Mouth, Pokol szája, and this lime alone survived. Crows then carried its seed and sowed the forest again, and a garabonciás, a protective spirit of Hungarian folklore, is said to live in the trunk. None of that is documented history; all of it is still told.

The castle is a hotel now, and its own blog describes the tree turning green every spring. The most recent dated report we have is from the 2012 contest, so if you have walked out to it, tell us how it looks.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the hollow base children climb through and the three thick limbs rising from it. It stands in the estate forest about a kilometre east of Bánó Mária Castle, beside the Malom-árok stream.

best_time.label: late June into July, when the old lime flowers

name: The Elm Tree of Căpeni

location.address: Beside the bridge over the Baraolt stream, north of Căpeni village, near road DJ131, Covasna county, Romania

access: Free, in an open field beside the road, reached by a short mowed path from DJ131; an information panel marks the tree, no restriction found
transport: Căpeni village, Covasna county, Szekler region; no rail, reached by car or regional bus along DJ131
story:
On 2 June 2018 a storm tore off one of this elm's three great limbs, and the tree kept going. It had already survived something far worse: the Dutch elm disease that killed more than three quarters of Europe's elms in the 20th century, spread by bark beetles.

The Elm of Căpeni, Köpec in Hungarian, won Romania's Tree of the Year in 2011 with 13,096 votes and came second in Europe in 2012 with 9,812. It stands in a field beside the bridge over the Baraolt stream, just north of the village and off road DJ131, in the Szekler country of Transylvania. It is over 35 metres tall and 7.3 metres round, and a 2011 Romanian news report puts its planting in the early 18th century, which makes it roughly 300 years old.

It has also come through the floods and fires of the Baraolt stream, though no source dates them. The damage from 2018 is not hidden: the broken limb was cut back and the wound sealed with a rubbery coating, and you can see it.

A travel writer who visited in September 2023 found a mowed path of about a hundred metres leading from the road through the field to the trunk, and an information panel with the tree's details, and suggested a stop of ten to fifteen minutes. That is about right for the tree, and a little short for the thought that a field elm this size is something most of Europe no longer has.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the sealed wound where one of its three main limbs came off in 2018, and by the information panel at its foot. It stands in the field beside the Baraolt stream bridge, reached by a mowed path from DJ131.
